slides.title: Product Life Cycle
slides.text: Product Life Cycle

A company’s products are born, grow, mature, and then decline, just as living things do
The product life cycle, reflects sales and profits of a product, over a period of time.
The product life cycle is the length of time that a product is available to customers. It starts when a product (a good or a service) is introduced into the market and ends when it's removed from the shelves.

slides.title: Introduction Phase
slides.text:
Introduction Phase
This phase marks the launch of the product in a market
Characteristics:
Introduction is a period of slow sales as the product is introduced in the market.
Profits are nonexistent in this stage because of the heavy expenses of product introduction.
Customers, who have low or no awareness of the product
Competition either does not exist or is limited to a few firms, who may also not be operating at efficient levels
During this phase, a firm’s requirement for cash is very high, hence, High Costs
Marketing Focus: To stimulate demand for the new product

slides.title: Marketing Strategies for Introduction Stage
slides.text:
Marketing Strategies for Introduction Stage
Product: Offer a basic product to ensure that it meets the market needs
Price: Penetration or Skimming price
Distribution: Build selective distribution
Promotion: Use heavy sales promotion to entice trial

bullets.text: Product: Offer a basic product to ensure that it meets the market needs

slides.title: Growth Phase
slides.text:
Growth Phase
Once a product crosses the introduction phase and customers have accepted the product, it enters the growth phase.
Characteristics:
Sales and profit grow exponentially
The market base expands, as more customers buy the product
Products that enter the growth phase, meet with a more strengthened and increased competition
There are lesser production bottlenecks and hence costs are relatively lower now.
Marketing Focus: Product modification, enlarging distribution and service network To attract more and more new customers.

slides.title: Maturity Phase
slides.text:
Maturity Phase
Most products that survive the heat of competition and gain customers’ approval enter the maturity phase. Characteristics:
This phase is characterized by slowing of growth rates of sales and profits. Profits and margins are at peak.
Period of stabilization in sales growth because the product has achieved acceptance by most potential buyers.
This phase is also marked by cut throat competition, which often tends to narrow down to a price and promotion war.
Marketing Focus: Differentiation, service augmentation, Intensive distribution

Marketing Strategies for Maturity Stage
Product: Diversify brand and models, Product Differentiation, Improved Features
Price: Price to match or beat competitors, Discounted price
Distribution: Build more intensive distribution
Promotion: Increase to encourage brand switching, Stress on brand differences and benefits

slides.title: Decline Phase
slides.text:
Decline Phase
This is the phase when sales decline, because customer preferences have changed in favour of more efficient and better products. Characteristics:
Sales fall off and profits drop
Number of competing firms gets reduced and generally the industry now has limited product versions available to the customer.
Marketing Focus: Milk the profitable segments, Withdrawal of products

slides.text:
Marketing Strategies for Decline Stage
Product: Phase out weak items
Price: Reduce Prices
Distribution: Go selective: phase out unprofitable outlets
Promotion: Reduce to level needed to retain hard-core loyals

slides.title: Innovators
slides.text:
Innovators
First group of people to try a new product
early adopters are willing to take risks.
This group is typically small, representing only small percentage of the population
Early Adopters
Group of people who try after innovators
They are often thought leaders and opinion leaders in their field
Less risky than innovators
Early Majority
As a product begins to have mass market appeal, the next class of adopter to arrive is the early majority.
Reasonably risk averse and wants to be sure that their resources are spent wisely on products.
Consider experiences of early adopters

slides.title: Brand Equity
slides.text:
Brand Equity
Brand equity
The set of assets linked to a brand’s name that subtracts from or adds to the value of the product or service.
Includes monetary value of a brand
Brand Equity can be Positive or Negative
A brand has positive brand equity when consumers react more favorably to it than to a generic or unbranded version of the same product. It has negative brand equity if consumers react less favorably than an unbranded version.
